\section{Conclusion}

This paper presents the first systematic per-example analysis of how attention affects cross-architecture agreement in hybrid recurrent models. Using the controlled model zoo of \citet{wang2025hybrid}, we compared three recurrent architectures across five attention ratios and two parameter scales. The central result is that aggregate performance convergence and per-example behavioral divergence are decoupled: these two quantities follow different trajectories as attention increases.

Three findings support this conclusion. First, attention-driven convergence is task-specific: among ten benchmarks, only LAMBADA, a pure context-retrieval task, shows monotonic reduction in cross-architecture variance. Reasoning and comprehension benchmarks show no such pattern. Second, convergence depends on scale. The 1.3B models exhibit complete monotonic convergence on LAMBADA, while the 340M models follow a non-monotonic trajectory with only partial variance reduction. Third, aggregate convergence and per-example divergence operate on different timescales. Cross-architecture variance on LAMBADA decreases gradually across attention ratios, but pairwise overlap between architectures' per-example effect sets saturates at the lowest attention level and does not increase further. The architectures reach similar overall scores through different per-example trade-offs.

These results carry a practical consequence for architecture selection. Choosing between recurrent backbones on the basis of aggregate benchmark scores can obscure per-example behavioral differences that persist after aggregate metrics converge. For deployment scenarios where per-input reliability matters, or for ensemble construction where member diversity determines error reduction, aggregate equivalence does not imply behavioral interchangeability. This observation connects to the underspecification framework of \citet{damour2022underspecification}: we quantify how architectural variation in hybrid recurrent models produces the same type of per-prediction divergence that prior work attributed to random initialization and training noise.

Several directions remain open. Interventional experiments, such as attention head ablation or cross-architecture head transplantation, could establish causal rather than observational links between attention and per-example effects. Additional scale points beyond 1.3B would clarify whether the convergence pattern extends or saturates at larger capacity. Testing other hybrid families such as Jamba and RWKV-6 would probe the generality of the decoupling across recurrent designs. Our analysis covers pretrained models only; fine-tuning may alter the dynamics reported here.

\section{Conclusion}

We present the first systematic per-example analysis of how attention affects cross-architecture agreement in hybrid recurrent models. The central result is that aggregate convergence and per-example divergence are decoupled: these two quantities follow different trajectories as attention increases.

Three findings support this conclusion. Convergence is task-specific: only LAMBADA shows monotonic reduction in cross-architecture variance among ten benchmarks. Convergence depends on scale: complete at 1.3B but partial and non-monotonic at 340M. Aggregate convergence and per-example divergence operate on different timescales: cross-architecture variance decreases gradually with attention, but per-example overlap saturates at the lowest attention level and does not increase further.

This connects to underspecification \citep{damour2022underspecification}: architectural variation produces per-prediction divergence analogous to what prior work attributed to random initialization.

Future work could establish causal links through attention head ablation, test generality across other hybrid families (Jamba, RWKV-6), and examine whether fine-tuning or additional scale points alter the decoupling pattern.
